verdict.tagline: Clunky menus and slow travel hide deep, rewarding monster combat.
for_you_if: you want deep combat against massive monsters
you enjoy experimenting with custom companion pawns
you have the patience for a slow opening
not_for_you_if: you expect modern fast travel systems
you rely heavily on keyboard and mouse controls
you are sensitive to clunky menu interfaces

claims.claim: Reviewers note that ultrawide resolutions are broken or locked to 16:9, cutting off parts of the display.

citations.review_text: If you have an ultra wide monitor, you WILL NOT be able to play the game in full screen. The aspect ratio is LOCKED to 16:9 and you WILL need to MOD the game to play full screen on a 21:9 ratio. It's funny how the game has a selection for ultra wide but still locks the aspect ratio to 16:9, effectively cutting off a large portion of your screen. When was this game released on PC and why hasn't there been a fix from CAPCOM? I had this game on my Switch and loved the game, unfortunately I was unable to finish the game since my switch was stollen so i figured I'll just play it on PC. I would only recommend this game to PC users whop do not have an ultra wide monitor.

bought this game a long time ago after having played on xbox. finally come back to play it today and the ultrawide resolutions are literally broken so part of the game is below screen and not visible. i can find no legit fix for this and its aparently a known problem that happened after a update.... very frustrating.  this is my only monitor and as of now this renders the game unplayable .

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the menu and character control systems as heavily controller-centric, making keyboard and mouse play feel poor.

citations.review_text:
I honestly can't fathom what these devs were thinking.

-- THE GOOD --

- Struggling to come up with anything here.

-- THE BAD --

- Why would anyone set Backspace to be the key that *saves* config changes? And why does the game take so long to save simple keybind remapping?
- Having 3 NPC companions made everything too hectic for a real-time game. 'This way! This way!'  And it seemed like the battles were pretty much over by the time I got to them if I didn't always run ahead of my party.
- That terrible theme song

-- THE UGLY --

- Why are so many keys reserved and unmappable? Had to use Power Toys to remap 8 different keys just to be able to play the game.
- When you select quit you have to sit through the opening splash screens and hear the awful theme song again before you can get back to the Start menu and select Exit

A lot of people love this game, but for me its trash. The menu system is like something from the dark ages of gaming on an Amiga (Great early computer BTW), and is clearly designed only for those using a controller (I do NOT use a controller. Ever. It loves to send you round in circles to get anything done, and actually trying to quit the game is something of a major task of returning to the main menu (like it or not) before finally being allowed to exit.

Character control is equally controller centric and while its quite possible on a keyboard/mouse combo, it feels quite bad as a result. Combat is ... strange. The camera loves to jump about and your character seems to want to wander off, attacking thin air half the time. When it is dark everything blinds you, especially magic.

I love a good RPG game, and this looks like it might have had some promise, but for me at least its just unplayable because everything is aimed at controllers.

cohorts.label: 2-20h
cohorts.summary: Reviewers struggle with direction, save confusion, and stamina drain during exploration, though combat and companions stand out.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the early game provides little direction, leaving players prone to wandering into high-level areas or struggling to know where to go next.

citations.review_text:
[h1]Such a love and hate one[/h1]

The game really gives you no guidance and unless you have friends who played it before, you can get to several unbeatable situations. I passed around bandits and stuck at higher-level location with barely any chance to get back.

+ Very impressive combat system
+ Skills, weapons, magic are passionate
+ Dorky helpers from other dimension
+ Cool monsters and bandits to fight
+ Curious world to explore

- Feels like 2007 MMO at times
- Too easy to ruin the playthrough

Game grew on me over time. Took a while to get into it. Didn't like it at first, but if you have patience, there's a solid game underneath. It's pretty old school - Drops you into the world, gives you little information or direction, and is fairly challenging in the early game. 
Combat can be fun - the fighter has a lot of move sets. Archer can play a bit like a shooter. Early game can be a slog - you'll spend a lot of time back-tracking, tryinng figure out what to do. There is no fast travel, and you get only 1 save file, so mistakes are time consuming. The story feels comically bare bones. 
Visually it's pretty solid. It's an old game, but the devs nailed the lighting and atmosphere - making the world look quite nice.

It goes on sale pretty cheap these days. If you're looking for an open world with decent combat, unique monsters, and don't mind the grind, then this might be for you.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the save and checkpoint system as confusing or awkward, noting that reloading or quitting can inadvertently cause significant loss of progress.

citations.review_text: Definitely like it! But... I just lost my HOURS of progress from the game. Minimum 10 HOURS! Decided to mess around and mess with the NPC and want to reload from last checkpoint. Brought me WAY back! Never knew that meant not the last one saved manually but rather the 'hard save' like resting at tavern, etc! Of course might be fine if I just quit without saving but accidentally pressed save and quit! I heard Dragon's Dogma 2 has similar save system so... WTF?! So what I like is... Well... It's a fantasy game with pretty fun gameplay and forming a party! Can't go wrong with that!

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the open world traversal and exploration can feel slow and repetitive due to limited fast travel and stamina draining outside of combat.

citations.review_text: Picked this up for cheap on the summer Steam sale after hearing really good things as well as that the reliable Capcom developed this series. In short the game’s combat and environment designs are great, the story is there but I felt like it wasn’t that interesting, and limited access to fast travel causes the back and forth traversal to feel repetitive over long stretches. For combat stats you get to start by choosing either melee, ranged or mage then later as you level up you get to upgrade to stronger classes of those roles or hybrids of each as well as unlock knew skill to use, equipment is also here and upgradable by using materials you find around the world. Movement and attacks in combat feel snappy and fluid although too much freedom comes at the cost of precision as there’s no lock on to target button causing certain boss fights where you need to target certain body parts more difficult then they should. This game does host a party of 4 and can be played in multiplayer but when playing alone you can you use other player’s characters as “pawns” controlled by AI in your party to fill the gaps. Like I said earlier in the story is there but it’s a simple hero chosen one story with not much character development or anything of real interest as I only played through the main quests maybe some of the side content offers more interesting stories. I do have to commend the great soundtrack as well as how all the game’s dialogue is voiced even if some accents sound silly sometimes. The villages, buildings and environments are detailed looks great even with dated graphics, traversing through everything is a joy to see the first time but after having to go back and forth multiple over these long distances does feel boring since there you can only fast travel when using a limited consumable item aside from the main city. It is also to be mentioned that there is also a whole epilogue/post game that offers a greater challenge and extra story that will probably double game …

Combat is okay even though it's clunkly. Pawn system is unique and interesting even though the lack of extensive controls of them are awful. There are many interesting skills, and the vocations are diverse and great. I don't have much to comment on exploration because I haven't explored that far, but It feels really slow with finite stamina (unlike in towns). I won't mind with the slower approach to incentive players into exploring, but the map is also genuinely ugly so it becomes annoying later on.

The plot and the narrative are incoherent and almost non-existent. I heard it gets better on the later part? But I won't even bother finishing the earlier parts when the first impression was already awful. Much of the introduction is filled vagueness, and they straight up drops you into the world without any proper world building as if you're already knew. The dialogues? They are bad, they're bad at conveying any emotion, they're bad at developing any characters, and they're also bad at giving directions. Voice acting is mediocre as well. 

Gameplay alone won't be able to carry me through the game.

Menu navigation is also dreadful on M & K and this was the nail in the coffin for me. I had to click on so many things (and press) just to access stuff. This was very apparent when I was trying to manage my inventory. The UI in general is also very dated.


This game genuinely has a very good blueprint, but they were ruined by poor execution.

4/10

[h3]5/10[/h3]

I really tried to love this game. In fact, I gave it two chances, five years apart, and dropped it both times.

Dragon's Dogma has an excellent combat system, creative vocations, and the Pawn system remains one of the most unique companion mechanics in any RPG. Fighting monsters is genuinely fun, and it's the main reason I kept playing for almost 20 hours on my second attempt.

Unfortunately, almost everything around that gameplay feels painfully dated. The UI is confusing, quality-of-life features are lacking, fast travel is restrictive, and navigation often feels frustrating. I had to look up guides multiple times simply because the game gave me little indication of what to do next.

The open world was my biggest disappointment. Exploration rarely feels rewarding, enemy variety is surprisingly limited, and you'll spend countless hours fighting the same goblins, wolves, bandits, and harpies. Stamina draining while sprinting outside combat only makes traveling even more tedious.

The story never hooked me, the characters left little impression, and many side quests feel repetitive or poorly designed. Escort missions, in particular, are some of the most frustrating I've played.

I can absolutely understand why this game became a cult classic, especially for those who played it when it released. But playing it for the first time today, it simply hasn't aged well enough for me.

If you're curious about the series, it's still worth experiencing, just be prepared for a game that shows its age in almost every aspect outside of its fantastic combat.

claims.claim: Reviewers state that the inventory system is clunky and frustrating due to strict weight limits and cumbersome menu navigation.

citations.review_text:

Dragon's Dogma was a game I enjoyed a lot as a teenager. It's a great concept and there are lots of cool things in the gameplay loop, such as climbing giant monsters, and very satisfying classes and skills. My favorites are Mystic Knight, Magick Archer, Warrior, and Strider. 

Due to how the encounters are designed most classes will not be equipped to handle every situation, at least not without going back to the Inn and re-selected skills or having prior knowledge of what skill are best for each area/quest. Oddly, Warrior gets only 3 skill slots while every other class has 6. This makes Warrior more difficult to play on top of having no ranged skills and very slow animations. If you want to play Warrior I highly recommend the Greatsword MAX mod by maxfriend23 on Nexus Mods.

The story has a lot of interesting concepts although you will have to talk to every NPC multiple times, and do every quest to understand all the details or just look it up. The way the story is presented to you through the main quests essentially gives you no information other than you are Arisen and must defeat the Dragon.

Gameplay feels fair for the most part (except the beginning if you start on Hard right away). However, the post-game content including the Bitterblack Isle expansion are huge difficulty spikes. That will require some grinding or a lot of patience. Once you conquer BBI though nothing can stop you. You'll find encounters in the base game that were tough now trivial 1 shot battles where you mop the floor with everyone. That always feels nice.

There are a lot of little annoyances and odd design choices, but it still makes for a fun experience. I have re-played DD:DA several times over the years and would still recommend it.

But why not load an earlier save then? Good question, the game only allows one save file, so I am stuck in a soft lock...

This is the original Dragon's Dogma and still the greatest. I've played this game on XBox 360, XBox One, and finally ran out of momentum on Steam. My enjoyment of the game lasted quite a long time, and through multiple playthroughs.

The game is hard, and it takes skill and sometimes cunning to get things to work the way you want them to. Battles are epic, from both your perspective and the enemy's. While a giant enemy can smash you to pieces in a strike or swallow you whole, you run the gamut between being a quick-and-agile death-by-a-thousand-cuts type enemy and being able to summon entire natural disasters on top of anyone who opposes you. Every fight is an absolute spectacle, and this game was created with just about everything attentive to the fighting. It will entertain you for a long time during and after.

The toughness, unfortunately, is not only relegated to the fights, however. Autosaves are few in-between, so it's possible to be out exploring when suddenly you come across a bandit encampment, get overpowered, and lose an hour of progress. This game is the enemy of the forgetful saver, but luckily you can save just about any time from the pause menu.

All-in-all, this is still a very satisfying game to play, and runs very light on modern hardware. If you have the time, enjoy this piece of gaming history, a hidden gem of its day, overshadowed by the release of Skyrim and forgotten for a long time. I hope you get at least as much enjoyment out of it as i did.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the game features a companion system consisting of customizable AI pawns that accompany the player.

citations.review_text:
A 2012 action RPG that aged so gracefully it's still sitting at "Very Positive" with 60,000+ reviews, beating its own 2024 sequel (which tanked on PC due to technical incompetence). Capcom made a game that knew exactly what it was: a deliberately janky, openly ambitious action RPG where the combat matters more than the story.

The real magic is the pawn system — AI companions you can customize, train, and squad-build like they're your personal lieutenants. They level with you, learn strategies, and get shared with other players' worlds, which creates this weird asynchronous multiplayer vibe where you're trading your pawns like Pokemon. It's mechanically brilliant and weirdly intimate for a 2012 game.

Nine different vocations (classes) with actual skill variety means you're not locked into one playstyle — respec constantly, experiment with hybrid builds, and watch how dramatically your AI squad adapts based on what you're throwing at them. The open world actively doesn't care if you're ready — enemies scale-gate you hard, which means overconfidence gets you demolished by a Griffin before you've seen the main story's first boss.

The story is generically medieval fantasy (evil Arisen, political intrigue, dark island expansion pack) and absolutely won't win writing awards. But the hundreds of hours of quests, the absurdly high replayability, and the fact that the PC version finally gave it the graphics polish the console versions never got? That's why people still play this instead of Dragon's Dogma 2.

Get it on sale for under $5 (it goes that low). The sequel cost $60 and is worse.
Looks great, and the support NPC system is fantastic. But there is stuff later on that I simply will not reveal.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the combat system as featuring distinct vocations, real-time climbing on large monsters to strike specific weak points, and magic casting that requires channel times.

citations.review_text:
One of the most unique fantasy RPGs I’ve ever played.

Dragon’s Dogma: Dark Arisen is genuinely one of the most memorable RPG experiences I’ve had. There are so many mechanics in this game that make it stand out from almost anything else in the genre.

The combat alone is incredible. Being able to physically grab onto larger enemies, climb across their bodies, and attack specific areas while they’re actively fighting you is such a cool mechanic. Magic is also handled extremely well. Playing as a spellcaster actually makes you feel powerful, with some of the most impressive and satisfying magic I’ve seen in a fantasy RPG.

There’s also a surprising amount of variety in how you can play. Different vocations, weapons, abilities, party setups, and playstyles can completely change how the game feels. I’ve put over 185 hours into it, played through the game more than once specifically to experience different builds and approaches, and I still never completely exhausted everything the game had to offer.

The world, story, and quests are also much deeper than they initially appear. Your decisions can actually have consequences, certain quests and actions can affect things later in the game, and there are plenty of moments where the game surprised me. I won’t spoil anything because this is absolutely a game that is better experienced blind.

It definitely has some quirks and shows its age in certain areas, but none of that stopped me from having an absolute blast with it.

For the amount of content, replayability, and genuinely unique ideas packed into this game, especially considering how cheap it regularly sells for, Dragon’s Dogma: Dark Arisen is an absolute must-buy in my opinion.

185+ hours played and I’d still recommend it without hesitation.

One of the best RPG i ever had

One of the few games that truly makes you feel like a real mage. Unlike most games where spells are cast instantly, every powerful spell in this game requires you to channeling spell first the more powerful spell the more time it needed to cast it, making magic feel authentic and immersive.

Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen is a game that took me some time to appreciate. My first experience with it was the PlayStation 3 version, and while I liked the atmosphere and the ideas behind the game, I had trouble fully getting invested in its world. It was only after returning to it several times that everything finally clicked. I have completely fallen in love with this title.

Because of that, I ended up buying the game on multiple platforms, but the PC version is easily the best way to experience it. The improved performance, higher resolution and much smoother gameplay make a huge difference compared to the original console releases.

Dragon's Dogma is not a perfect game, but it is one of the most unique RPGs created by Capcom. The strongest part of the experience is definitely the combat system. Every class plays completely differently, which makes experimenting with different vocations extremely satisfying. Whether you prefer magic, heavy weapons, ranged attacks or fast melee combat, every style gives you a different way to approach enemies.

The battles against large monsters are especially memorable. Fighting a dragon, griffin or another massive creature feels completely different from fighting groups of goblins or lizard-like enemies. Climbing on enemies, attacking weak points and working together with your pawns creates some of the most spectacular encounters in any action RPG.

The Dark Arisen expansion adds even more depth to the game. Bitterblack Isle introduces a much darker dungeon-focused experience and creates an addictive gameplay loop: exploring deeper, defeating powerful enemies, farming better equipment and returning again to challenge the final boss of the expansion. It gives the game a reason to keep playing long after finishing the main story.

The pawn system is another feature that makes Dragon's Dogma stand out. Creating your own companion and recruiting other players' pawns gives the adventure a unique feeling.

Great game. Particularly for old school RPG fans because of its slow pace. Warning, You have to walk ALLOT.  inexperienced or younger players this may throw them off. As you play through you get two items called portcrystals that you can set anywhere to fast travel back and forth too in addition to your hometown and the capital where the Gran Duke is. The game has 9 Vocations or jobs, 3 only for the main character called the Arisen, and the other 6 your pawns (look alike humans from this area called The Rift) can use. Fighter/Warrior, Strider/Ranger, MAge/Sorceror, And the hybrid classes Mystic Knight, Magic Archer and Assasin  exclusive to The Arisen.
 
Combat is similar to Skyrim only in third person. Hitboxes are very accurate relative to the size of whatever your fighting (means you can hit any part of them and it will do damage relative to how durable that part is). You Also climb large monsters like Cyclops and Chimeras to get to their eyes, head etc. All these require stamina which drains everytime you run or perform moves during fights (Hint: Striders/Rangers gain the most stamina as they level up, double what Mages/Sorcerors/ or Warriors/Fighters do if you want to stamina max before switching vocations which you can do).As You play through, you will run out of stamina pretty frequently during fights because sometimes you forget there is a stamina bar as you fight. Your pawn has two Inclinations that will determine how they fight and will be determined how you give commands using the directional buttons. Your commands direct there general behavior, not if and when they attack. For example if they stay near to to make sure your okay or go and kill enemies regardless of where you are. You can change this via the knowledge chair thats at every Inn or camp.

The story is more or less straight forward. Every number of generations this dragon comes to terrorize the land. this person born called the Arisen with this strange connection to the dragon is called forth …

citations.review_text: Underrated gem of a game. Mixes Witcher, Dark Souls, and Monster Hunter to create a truly unique and satisfying experience. Still holds up well. It's unique mechanic of being able to grab onto most living things offers a very dynamic and creative combat experience which is surprisingly absent in most games. It's AI companion systems - "Pawns", is a lovely system and is surpsingly fleshed out. This game has classes that are not seen in most games. I have a lot more hours in this game than what my account shows - likely double the play time.

This game is simultaneously as shallow as a puddle and as deep as a large lake. The world and characters are cardboard standees. The vocation system is neat. Its balancing systems are also at odds with one another. The combat is somewhat unique and I find it fun (after the low-level BS), but the game is chock full of janky, unsatisfying, and messy design that has no respect for your time. (And no, I'm mostly not talking about trekking across the map, as I know how to use Port crystals, and the DA version at least gives you the Infinite Ferrystone since they realized limiting it to consumable stones was a terrible idea with their amusement park-like map and awful quest design).

It's like Oblivion, except the alchemy system is SO MUCH WORSE. It's like Kingdoms of Amalur, both in the Destinies/Vocations feeling and playing quite distinctly, and in that the combat can be fast and fun, and allow for tactical engagement and varied approaches. In that way, this actually feels a little deeper, but less focused. Then there are the pawns. Engaging and tactically useful, but can be frustrating from their stupidity and jank as often as they come in clutch. The tandem party synergy is fun to put together for different enemy types, though. The problem is that it's completely unclear how to make them do what you want them to do.

The opening cutscene also looks like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ due to horrible PS2-quality textures and material and lighting rendering. It basically only looks …

a pretty average game overall, brimming with potential but brought down by a lack of polish and an apparent lack of dev time/budget. the middling story, forgettable characters and relatively shallow worldbuilding may put off most players, but the exploration is nice, the progression is satisfying, the combat is one-of-a-kind and the dlc area offers a great challenge with new encounters and even better progression. the pawn system is also incredibly unique and creates depth in party building and strategic planning, even if the ai itself is not all that great and oftentimes frustrating.

it's not the best game, but when it hits, it HITS. a pretty good investment, as it goes on sale very often.

When I first tried DD some years ago I didn't like it. It was a strange and cofusing mess of a game of the like that I never played before, so I quit. But since then I kept wanting to play it again and finaly did, and this time DD clicked.

I'll keep it as short as possible.
Some may compare DD to Monster Hunter, but I have never played any MH before, so let me describe the game like this:

- DD is an Action RPG (think Diablo and the like) but in 3rd person, set in a small but condenced Open World for you to grind Exp and Loot to get better and stronger, while returning to town with a ''town portal'' to unload your loot and restock on heals + resting to reset mob spawn. DD has a dynamic day/night system with mobs related to it. This game is a grinders/hoarders paradise.

- DD also has JRPG roots heavily coded into its dna. The vocations are your Final Fantasy job system. The main game where you need to defeat the main bad ''guy'' only to learn that nothing is what it seems and go into post-game to defeat the real threat. And the Expansion - Dark Arisen is your typical optional endgame hardest dungeon to conquer. And many more design similarities.

Once Dragon's Dogma clicks, it can become unbelievably addicting.
